title: ‘Never the same’: How war on Iran changed the global energy sector
facts: The United States and Israel launched a war on Iran in late February 2026.
Approximately one-fifth of global oil and liquefied natural gas supplies normally pass through the Strait of Hormuz during peacetime.
The United States and Iran signed a memorandum of understanding on June 17, 2026, regarding the safe passage of vessels in the Strait of Hormuz.
Maritime traffic in the Strait of Hormuz reached a post-war peak of more than 70 transits on June 24, 2026.
Attacks on two commercial ships in the Strait of Hormuz over the final weekend of June 2026 caused a sharp drop in maritime traffic.
Energy suppliers have increased the use of Saudi Arabia’s East-West Pipeline to bypass the Strait of Hormuz.
Around 20 million barrels of oil moved through the Strait of Hormuz each day before the outbreak of the 2026 war.
Simon Stiell serves as the top United Nations climate official.
Simon Stiell stated in April 2026 that the conflict involving Iran was supercharging the global renewables boom.
Global renewable energy capacity reached a record high in 2025 according to the International Renewable Energy Agency.
Non-fossil fuel projects accounted for approximately 86 percent of added global power capacity in 2025.
China produces more than 80 percent of the world’s wind turbines, solar panels, and energy storage batteries.
Wood Mackenzie is a research and consulting company tracking renewable energy component production.
Maurice Obstfeld is a senior fellow at the Peterson Institute for International Economics.
The United States is strengthening its position as a swing supplier of liquefied natural gas due to the geopolitical shifts following the Iran war.
